name: Golden Brown
lede: Golden brown is a rich yellowy brown, a name Paterson links to hair and to the lichen called crottle.

sections.title: A plain description
sections.body:
Paterson defines golden brown as a rich yellowy-brown [1]. He also notes that auburn can mean a brownish red or sometimes golden-brown, especially for hair, and that the old word crottle named the golden-brown of lichen [1]. In his colour-name lists it sits among the browns beside [[caramel]], [[bistre]], [[chocolate]] and [[tawny]] [1].

The swatch here is ISCC-NBS block 57, a strong yellowish brown, cited from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary [2]. It is also on the xkcd list from 2010 [2].

sections.title: Dye and paint
sections.body: Balfour-Paul's glossary notes that weld, the European yellow dye plant, gives a golden-brown textile dye, often combined with indigo resist [3]. Ball describes Morris Louis's veil paintings of the late 1950s, where repeated bright layers poured thin fused to a warm golden-brown [4]. In both cases the color is the result of layering, not a single pigment.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color appears in 1,054 of 23,781 archive paintings, more common than 85 percent of named colors, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent in 60 percent of 628 [5]. Fritz Thomsen is its most devoted painter, in 5 of 18 works [5]. It peaks in the 1300s at 6.4 percent of 251 paintings, 2.8 times the baseline [5]. The earliest match is 1230, about 700 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1930 [5]. As photographed, aged varnish can push many colors toward this look-alike hue.
